https://www.coventrytelegraph.net/news/l.text: A woman who suffered years of abuse at the hands of her former partner has described how she was left feeling 'completely worthless' as he was jailed. She had initially been in a 'loving' relationship with Abbas Mohammed, but said it turned into a cycle of fear, violence and threats. Mohammed admitted a campaign of controlling and coercive behaviour against the woman and was jailed for more than three years at Warwick Crown Court . As reported by CoventryLive , the pair began seeing each other casually at the end of 2020 before becoming a couple in February 2021. What began as a relationship the victim described as 'kind and loving' quickly changed as Mohammed became increasingly controlling. She said 'red flags' started to appear as the 38-year-old grew 'loud, cocky and arrogant'. READ MORE: Court update on Latvian national charged over death of Keaton Slater READ MORE: Coventry MP says 'long journey' finally sees Keaton Slater suspect back in UK Warwick Crown Court was told how Mohammed described himself as a 'narcissist' in messages while keeping images of her and growing increasingly jealous. She described one incident in which he became angry after believing three men were looking at her and began throwing items around. He told her: “ You are not the pristine girl that I want. ” In 2023, Mohammed headbutted the victim and took £800 from her savings, which had been put aside for Christmas gifts. Mohammed also told the victim to kill herself before she attempted to take her own life in October 2024. He further exerted control over the woman by calling her 'my little victim.' One of the most serious physical assaults took place in November 2024, when Mohammed punched the woman in the face and kicked her as she lay on the ground. She was left with a split lip and serious bruising. She said she found herself trapped in a relationship where she was constantly monitored, insulted and threatened. Prosecutor Ammo Khanna said Mohammed called the woman vile names, including 'sl*g' and 'wh*re' and accused her of being 'psychologically unstable.' Warwick Crown Court was told the woman was forced to send photographs showing where she was when out with her kids. Mohammed also frequently interrogated her about who was liking her social media posts. But the abuse extended beyond her as Mohammed sent 'insulting' messages to the father of her children and behaved aggressively towards her parents. She said he also claimed to know 'dangerous Albanians' who could come after her if she reported his behaviour, Warwick Crown Court heard. In July 2025, Mohammed hit her head against the steering wheel while they were in a car together, Warwick Crown Court was told. He also threatened to 'expose her' on a podcast if she told anyone about what had happened. Ms Khanna said Mohammed focused on his own mental health struggles while showing little empathy for the impact his actions had. He claimed he had written a 400-page book about his experiences and said he had also been abused. In a statement read to Warwick Crown Court , the victim said the hardest part had been accepting that the person she loved was not who she thought he was. She described feeling trapped in a cycle that was 'never going to end' and said she stayed silent because she feared what he was capable of. Ms Khanna said the victim described feeling 'completely worthless and scared' and that every part of her life had been affected. She said she developed mental health problems and that thoughts of taking her own life had also returned. Mohammed, of Crowsfurlong, Rugby , was jailed for three years and two months at Warwick Crown Court on July 30. Judge Anthony Potter said the impact of his behaviour would remain with the victim 'for the foreseeable future' as the abuse had left lasting emotional scars. Defending, Amrita Marwaha said Mohammed had been experiencing significant emotional distress at the time of the offending. She said he was 'remorseful' for his actions and had taken steps to address his behaviour while on remand. https://khak.com/eighth-avenue-bridge-re.text: Cedar Rapids Unveils Plans to Replace Nearly 90-Year-Old Bridge Cedar Rapids Unveils Plans to Replace Nearly 90-Year-Old Bridge Ryan "Brain" Brainard Ryan "Brain" Brainard Published: August 27, 2026 Canva/Google Maps Share on Facebook Share on Twitter The city of Cedar Rapids is making plans to replace a bridge that has carried cars across the Cedar River for nearly 90 years. The public got its first chance to see those plans this week. Replacing The 8th Avenue Bridge The city of Cedar Rapids is preparing to replace the 8th Avenue bridge that has stood for nearly 90 years, according to CBS2 . The newly proposed bridge would stand some 15 feet higher to better work with the city's flood control system. Members of the community got a chance to see details of the project on Wednesday, which is expected to begin next year. What Will The New Bridge Look Like? Rob Davis, the city of Cedar Rapids flood control system manager , told CBS2 that the new bridge sits up higher so "we’ll be able to go over the top of the flood control system walls. And then when we do that, that will allow for transportation element during a flood." The new bridge will be a cable-stayed bridge with four lanes for traffic, and pedestrian lanes on both sides. City of Cedar Rapids, Iowa Government City of Cedar Rapids, Iowa Government How Much Will The Project Cost? CBS2 reports that the price tag for the new 8th Avenue bridge will be $123 million, including the work on the bridge and work on the floodwall. $62.4 million will come from grants from the U.S. Department of Transportation and another $1 million from a state grant. The rest of the cost will be covered by local flood mitigation funds and bonds. The bridge will remain closed for the duration of the project. Photograph: Guillaume Horcajuelo/EPA Gisèle Pelicot ‘Jaw-dropping’ play based on Pelicot rape trial comes to London for one night Four-hour production featuring star-studded cast will be performed at London County Hall Helena Horton Tue 29 Sep 2026 03.00 EDT Last modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 06.59 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A play based on the trial of the men who drugged and raped Gisèle Pelicot will come to London for one night only this November – and promises to feature a star-studded cast. The four-hour production of The Pelicot Trial: Tribute to Gisèle Pelicot has been performed around the world, including in New York City and Avignon, the city in France where the trial took place. This autumn, it is coming to London County Hall, the home of Agatha Christie’s Witness for the Prosecution. “I saw it in French originally – all four hours of it. It was jaw-dropping, harrowing, really emotional,” said Nadia Fall, artistic director and co-chief executive of the Young Vic, which is putting on the performance. “It was the act of witnessing that really got me: it is long-form and testimonial in form.” Fall expects the show to sell out immediately. “Because it’s one night only, what we are able to do is ring our best actors, people you will know ‘off the telly’ as well,” Fall said. The full cast will be announced before tickets go on sale in the coming weeks. Fall added: “The ensemble rehearses together just once. That allows you to call up the best of people who are available for a short commitment. I really can’t wait to announce the company. It is, I think, 27 actors all in all.” The play was created by Milo Rau and Servane Dècle. The Swiss director and playwright Rau is known for adapting court cases for the stage, including the Moscow trial of the Russian punks Pussy Riot and the trial of the Romanian despot Nicolae Ceaușescu. Pelicot became internationally recognised after she waived her right to anonymity to ensure a public trial of her ex-husband, Dominique Pelicot, who, for almost a decade from 2011, drugged her unconscious and invited dozens of men from an internet forum to rape her . Her husband was sentenced to 20 years in prison in December 2024 and guilty verdicts were returned for all 51 accused men. She wanted the story to be public, saying “shame must change sides”. “We do it one time only in each city,” said Rau. “It is more of a political act really, than a play.” “It is a harsh watch,” said Dècle, “but people stay for the whole time. We let them come in and out if they want, but very few do. Even Gisèle Pelicot herself came to watch in New York. That was amazing. She said, ‘The actress was doing better than I did on trial.’” Journalists covering the trial gave Rau and Dècle thousands of pages of their notebooks, and the play is based on what was said in court. “Everyone wanted to share with us,” said Rau. “It became a trial of our society, of the patriarchy. And we have toured it in at least 15 different countries, in different languages, some I barely understand myself, and the audience still understands the play. Sadly it is a universal experience. It would be better for humanity if this was just a French experience.” skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to The Guide Get our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every Friday after newsletter promotion “It isn’t scenes and costumes in a set like a traditional piece of theatre. It is the facts. It just floors you,” said Fall. The large majority of the audience has been female, Dècle said. “I wish more men would see it. The very interesting thing about this whole affair is you can really dive into who these male perpetrators were.” Fall said: “Pelicot represents so much for everybody, especially women; resilience and courage and a radical joy for me that she triumphed and lives on. She’s in love and lives her life. That is two fingers up to the patriarchy and I think that is really empowering for us women. This piece and her story is not just about the specifics about her story and sexual assault.” She agreed to the play, the writers said, because she wanted to keep the conversation that was started by her trial going. “We always say she opened the door, and we just keep it open,” said Rau.
